back: Centralizes and automates backup policies (schedule, retention, cross-region/cross-account copy) across EBS, RDS, DynamoDB, EFS, FSx, and more from one place, instead of configuring native backup features per-service separately — the answer whenever a scenario wants one unified backup policy/compliance story across many resource types.

Network-attached block storage for EC2, tied to a single AZ (must snapshot to move across AZs — snapshots are stored in S3 behind the scenes).

Volume types matter on the exam: gp3 (general purpose baseline), io2/io2 Block Express (highest IOPS, for latency-sensitive/critical DBs), st1 (throughput-optimized HDD for big sequential workloads like big data), sc1 (cold HDD, cheapest, infrequent access).

Continuously replicates on-premises or cloud servers to a low-cost staging area in AWS, allowing fast (minutes) failover/recovery during a disaster — AWS's current recommended DR tool, effectively superseding the older CloudEndure Disaster Recovery branding.

Managed, fully elastic NFS file system that many EC2 instances (and Lambda functions) can mount concurrently across multiple AZs — unlike EBS, which attaches to only one instance at a time (except io2 Multi-Attach in narrow cases).

Exam trigger: 'shared file storage accessible by multiple Linux instances simultaneously' points to EFS, not EBS.

Family of managed third-party file systems: FSx for Windows File Server (SMB, AD-integrated, for Windows workloads), FSx for Lustre (high-performance parallel file system for HPC/ML, can link directly to S3 as a data repository), FSx for NetApp ONTAP, and FSx for OpenZFS.

Exam trigger: pick the specific FSx variant matching the workload's native file system requirement (e.g. Lustre for HPC/ML, Windows File Server for AD-joined Windows apps).

Object storage with 11 nines of durability, unlimited scale.

Storage classes trade cost for retrieval speed/frequency: Standard (frequent access), Standard-IA/One Zone-IA (infrequent access, cheaper storage + retrieval fee), Intelligent-Tiering (auto-moves objects between tiers based on access patterns — no retrieval fee, ideal for unpredictable access), and the Glacier family for archival.

Lifecycle policies automate transitions/expirations — a very frequent exam cost-optimization pattern.

front: Amazon S3 Glacier (S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval / Deep Archive)
back: Lowest-cost long-term archival storage classes within S3.

Hybrid storage connecting on-premises applications to AWS storage via standard protocols: File Gateway (NFS/SMB backed by S3), Volume Gateway (iSCSI block volumes, cached or stored mode, backed by EBS snapshots in S3), and Tape Gateway (virtual tape library backed by S3/Glacier, for replacing physical backup tape infrastructure).

Exam trigger: 'on-premises application needs to use AWS storage without being rewritten' via a familiar protocol.

front: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval vs. Deep Archive — what's the retrieval tradeoff?
back:
Flexible Retrieval: minutes (Expedited) to hours (Standard/Bulk).

Deep Archive: cheapest tier, 12-hour standard retrieval — meant for compliance archives rarely if ever accessed.

AWS defines four DR strategies, ordered by increasing cost and decreasing RTO/RPO: Backup and Restore, Pilot Light, Warm Standby, and Multi-Site Active/Active. Each has its own card with the specific trade-off, but the ordering itself is the exam-critical fact: cheaper strategies accept longer recovery times and more potential data loss, while faster recovery always costs more to run standing infrastructure in the DR Region.

The cheapest and slowest strategy: back up data (and infrastructure-as-code templates) to another Region, but run nothing there until a disaster actually happens — then restore from backups and provision infrastructure from scratch.

RTO: hours. RPO: depends on backup frequency, typically hours. Appropriate when cost matters far more than downtime.

Critical core infrastructure (e.g. a database) is always running and continuously replicating data to the DR Region, but the rest of the application (compute, etc.) is switched off — scaled up only when a failover is triggered.

RTO: tens of minutes. RPO: seconds to minutes, since data replication is continuous. Cheaper than Warm Standby because most compute stays off until needed.

A scaled-down but fully functional copy of the entire application always runs in the DR Region — not just the database like Pilot Light, but application servers too, just at lower capacity. On failover, it scales up to handle full production traffic.

RTO: minutes. RPO: seconds. More expensive than Pilot Light since compute is always running, but recovers faster.

The full production workload runs simultaneously in two (or more) Regions, actively serving live traffic in both — not just standing by. Failover means routing traffic away from the failed Region, since the other Region is already handling load.

RTO: near-zero. RPO: near-zero. The most expensive strategy, since you're running full duplicate production capacity continuously — but it's also the only one with no failover delay at all.

Lets you define an application's RTO and RPO targets, then assesses the actual architecture against them — running standardized tests (e.g. simulating an AZ failure) and scoring how well it would actually meet those targets, with specific recommendations to close any gap.

Think of it as the tool that validates whether your chosen DR strategy is actually implemented correctly, rather than just assumed to work.

Locks a backup vault into WORM (write-once-read-many) mode — once enabled, no one, including the AWS account root user, can delete backups or shorten their retention period before it expires. Governance mode allows a small set of privileged users to still remove the lock; compliance mode makes it irreversible even for AWS.

The standard answer whenever a scenario needs backups that are provably immune to deletion, e.g. for ransomware protection or regulatory retention requirements.

A named network endpoint attached to a bucket with its own IAM policy, letting you manage access for many different applications or teams sharing one bucket without editing a single, ever-growing bucket policy. Each access point can also be restricted to a specific VPC, blocking access from outside it entirely.

A single global endpoint that routes S3 requests to the lowest-latency replica of a bucket across multiple Regions, using AWS Global Accelerator's network under the hood. Requires S3 Cross-Region Replication between the underlying buckets — MRAP is the unified front door, not the replication mechanism itself.

Attaches a Lambda function to S3 GET (and increasingly other) requests, transforming the object's contents on the fly before returning it — e.g. redacting PII, resizing an image, or converting a file format — without creating and storing a separate transformed copy of the object.

Speeds up long-distance uploads/downloads to/from an S3 bucket by routing traffic through the nearest CloudFront edge location and over AWS's private backbone network the rest of the way, instead of the public internet the whole route.

Exam nuance: it accelerates transfer over a given connection, but it doesn't change the connection's own available bandwidth — if the underlying link itself is the bottleneck (e.g. a slow last-mile connection), Transfer Acceleration won't fix a multi-month transfer timeline the way a physical Snow Family device would.
